script.opening: “Hi. I’ve had loads of letters about Isla and Leo’s jabs — and now there’s one about measles at the nursery. I’m not one of those anti-vaccine people, I just… it’s complicated. I wanted to talk to someone before I book anything.”

facts.text: If asked what happened before: “After her first jabs she had a temperature of 39.4 and screamed for hours. I ended up at the out-of-hours place at midnight. She was fine by the next day, but I was terrified.” No seizure, no floppiness, no rash or swelling of face or lips, no breathing problems.
“She had the 8, 12 and 16 week ones. I gave her Calpol after the second and third ones like they said, and she was fine.” Missed the 12-month and 18-month ones.
“He had all his baby ones and his one-year ones. He hasn’t had the pre-school one — that was when the nurse upset me.”
“My friend says chickenpox is better to catch naturally, get it over with. And this MMRV is new, isn’t it? Is it tested?”
“Isn’t it a lot for a little body, three or four injections in one go?”
Both well. No allergies. No medical conditions, no steroids or other medicines. Neither has had chickenpox. No one at home has a weakened immune system. Kezia is not pregnant.
If asked what makes it hard to come: “I’m on a zero-hours contract — if I don’t work, I don’t get paid. The appointments are always weekday mornings. I can’t do two separate trips.”
If asked about previous experiences or what put her off: “Last time the nurse said I was putting other kids at risk. I felt like a bad mum. I didn’t want to go back.”
“The nursery letter said there were cases. That scared me — I know measles can be bad.”

Guarded at first, ready to feel judged. If the doctor lectures or quotes statistics without listening, get defensive (“See, this is why I didn’t come”). If the doctor asks about your experiences and acknowledges the scary night with Isla, relax and engage. Accept a catch-up plan if your questions about fever, “too many” and chickenpox are answered and the appointment problem is solved. You may ask whether you could have MMR instead of MMRV for Isla — be open to either once it is explained.

ice.ideas: Vaccines are mostly good, but her daughter reacts badly and chickenpox might be better caught naturally.
ice.concerns: Another frightening fever; overloading her daughter; being judged as a bad parent; losing pay.
ice.expectations: Honest answers and some control over the plan — not to be told off.

cues: “I’m not one of those anti-vaccine people” — she expects judgement.
“It’s complicated” — there is more than the medical worry.
Sighs when appointment times come up.

checkpoints.text: Establishes which vaccines each child has had and missed, using the record, and confirms health status (allergies, immunosuppression, previous chickenpox)
Takes a history of the previous reaction and distinguishes an expected febrile reaction from a true contraindication (anaphylaxis)
Explores her reasons in an open, non-judgemental way, including previous experiences of care and practical barriers
Explains the catch-up accurately — no need to restart, missed doses can be given now, several vaccines can be given at one visit, MMRV for Isla, pre-school booster and second MMR for Leo
Gives balanced information on benefits and risks, including fever management and why chickenpox can be serious, and mentions that MMR can be offered instead of MMRV if she prefers
Arranges a practical appointment (out-of-hours or Saturday clinic, both children together) and follows up, documenting her decisions respectfully
Acknowledges the frightening night with Isla and the previous negative experience without defending or criticising colleagues
Shares the decision — checks what she wants to do, respects her choice, and leaves the door open

worked.txt: “Lots of parents have questions — I’m glad you came to ask them. I’m not here to tell you off.”

“That sounds like a really frightening night. A high fever after the 8-week jabs is a known effect of the MenB vaccine in babies — it’s why we give paracetamol. It isn’t an allergy and it doesn’t mean she’ll react like that again.”
“Children’s immune systems deal with thousands of germs every day. Giving several vaccines at one visit is safe and means fewer trips for you.”

“Most children get through chickenpox fine, but some get serious skin infections, pneumonia or brain inflammation, and it means a week off nursery — and work for you. MMRV has been used for years in other countries.”
“If you’d prefer the MMR without chickenpox for Isla, that can be arranged — though MMRV is what we recommend.”
“Could we book both of them together at our Saturday clinic?”

f.learning: Behind most missed vaccinations are practical barriers and specific worries, not refusal. Explore without judgement, using open questions, and ask about past experiences of care. A fever after the 8-week vaccines is common (especially with MenB) and is not a contraindication; true contraindications are rare (confirmed anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component; live vaccines in significant immunosuppression or pregnancy). Catch-up principles: never restart a course; give missed doses as soon as possible; several vaccines can be given at the same visit. Since 1 January 2026, MMRV has replaced MMR in the routine schedule at 12 and 18 months for children born on or after 1 January 2025; UKHSA allows MMR to be offered where a parent prefers it. Leo needs his pre-school booster and second MMR-containing dose. Make access easy (combined, out-of-hours appointments) and document the parent’s decisions.

wordPics.clearPass: Creates a non-judgemental space, uncovers the febrile reaction, the previous negative experience and the work barrier, answers each worry accurately (fever, multiple vaccines, chickenpox, MMRV vs MMR), explains catch-up for both children, and agrees a practical joint appointment that she chooses.
wordPics.pass: Explores the main concern and gives accurate catch-up information with a practical plan; the previous negative experience or access barrier is addressed less fully.
wordPics.fail: Gives accurate facts but in a lecturing way, or does not establish what each child needs; misses the access barrier; plan left to “book with reception”.
wordPics.clearFail: Judgemental or coercive (“you’re putting other children at risk”), gives inaccurate information (for example that the course must restart or that a previous fever is a contraindication), or no plan.

avoid.dont: “You’re putting other children at risk by not vaccinating.”
avoid.instead: “Can you tell me what’s made it hard to get them done?”
avoid.why: Blame drives parents away; she has already experienced this.

avoid.dont: “The science is settled — there’s nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “That’s a really reasonable question — let me explain what we know.”
avoid.why: Dismissing concerns reduces trust; specific answers build it.

avoid.dont: “We’ll have to start the course again.”
avoid.instead: “We don’t need to start again — we just pick up where we left off.”

model.text: Hello Kezia, I’m Dr Ahmed. Thank you for booking — I know you’ve had a few letters. I’m not here to tell you off; I’d like to hear what’s been going on.
I’m not anti-vaccine. It’s just complicated.
Tell me about it — what’s made it complicated?
After Isla’s first jabs she had 39.4 and screamed for hours. I ended up at out-of-hours at midnight.
That sounds frightening. Did she have any swelling of her face or lips, breathing problems, a rash, or a fit?
model.why: Distinguishes febrile reaction from anaphylaxis or febrile seizure

model.text: No, just the temperature and crying. She was fine the next day.
Has anything else put you off — anything about previous appointments?
Last time the nurse said I was putting other kids at risk. I felt like a bad mum. And I’m on zero hours — weekday mornings mean no pay.

I’m sorry that happened — you came for help and left feeling judged. That’s not what we want. Can I check: has either child had chickenpox, any allergies, or any illness or medicines that affect the immune system?
model.why: Acknowledges the experience without criticising a colleague; checks safety

model.text: No chickenpox, no allergies, both healthy.

The fever Isla had is a known effect of the MenB vaccine in babies — it’s why paracetamol is given. It isn’t an allergy and doesn’t stop her having the rest. The 12- and 18-month vaccines are less likely to cause that kind of fever, though she might have a mild temperature or rash about a week after the MMRV.
model.why: Accurate, reassuring explanation of the reaction and what to expect

model.text: Isn’t it too much, several in one go? And my friend says chickenpox is better caught naturally.

Children’s immune systems handle thousands of germs a day, so several vaccines at once is safe and saves you trips. Most children get through chickenpox fine, but some get bad skin infections, pneumonia or brain inflammation — and it means a week off nursery and work. Since January the NHS gives the MMRV to protect against it.
Can she have the old one, without chickenpox?

Yes, if you prefer, she can have MMR instead — though we recommend MMRV. We don’t need to restart anything: Isla needs her missed 12- and 18-month vaccines, a month apart, and Leo needs his pre-school booster and second MMR.
What would you like to do? And what would make it easiest — we have a Saturday clinic where both could be seen together.
Saturday would be good. I’ll go with the MMRV for Isla — I don’t want her getting chickenpox if it can be bad.

I’ll book a longer slot with our nurse who does the children’s clinic and note your concerns so you don’t have to repeat yourself. Paracetamol can be given if they have a fever afterwards; if either child seems very unwell after the vaccines, call us or 111. And if you change your mind about anything, just let us know.
model.why: Arranges, documents respectfully, safety-nets and leaves the door open

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA Immunisation against infectious disease (Green Book), chapters 11 (schedule) and 34 (varicella) · UKHSA MMRV programme: information for healthcare professionals (January 2026) · UKHSA Vaccination of individuals with uncertain or incomplete immunisation status (current) · NICE NG218 Vaccine uptake in the general population (2022)
knowledge.summary: Children who have missed vaccines should catch up without restarting courses. Since 1 January 2026, MMRV replaces MMR at 12 and 18 months for children born on or after 1 January 2025. Explore hesitancy respectfully and remove practical barriers.

points.t: From 1 January 2026, MMRV is given at 12 months and at a new 18-month appointment (born on or after 1 January 2025). Children born 1 July–31 December 2024 have MMR at 12 months then MMRV. A selective varicella catch-up for older eligible pre-school children is planned. UKHSA allows MMR to be offered where a parent prefers it.

Do not restart an interrupted course. Give missed doses as soon as possible with the correct minimum intervals (MMR/MMRV doses at least 4 weeks apart). Several vaccines can be given at one visit in different sites.
Fever is common after MenB in infants; prophylactic paracetamol is recommended with MenB doses under 1 year. Fever is not a contraindication to further doses.

Confirmed anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component. Live vaccines (MMR, MMRV) are not given in significant immunosuppression or pregnancy. Minor illness without fever is not a reason to delay.

Usually mild in children but can cause secondary bacterial skin infection (including invasive group A streptococcal disease), pneumonia, encephalitis and, rarely, death. It also causes missed nursery and parental work.
Highly infectious; complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and death. Two doses of an MMR-containing vaccine give about 99% protection.
Use open questions, acknowledge concerns, give specific information, and avoid blame. NICE recommends flexible appointment times and making every contact count.
At 3 years 4 months: 4-in-1 (DTaP/IPV) and second dose of MMR (MMRV depending on date of birth and current guidance).

social.t: Zero-hours work and single trips matter. Offer combined, evening or weekend appointments.

legal.t: Vaccination of children needs consent from a person with parental responsibility; it is voluntary in the UK. Record the decision and the information given.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: treat patients with respect and without judgement. Acknowledge a poor previous experience without blaming colleagues; consider feedback to the team.

community.t: NHS vaccinations pages; UKHSA “MMRV — information for parents” leaflet; Vaccine Knowledge Project (Oxford).

Pregnancy (for the parent, re: live vaccines in contacts — not a contraindication)

playbook.diagnosis: Two children with missed routine vaccinations (Isla: 12- and 18-month incl. MMRV; Leo: pre-school booster and MMR2); hesitancy after an expected febrile reaction and a negative experience; access barriers.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Neither of them needs to start again. Isla needs her two missed sets, a month apart, and Leo needs his pre-school jabs. The fever Isla had was a known side effect, not an allergy.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re not against vaccines — you were frightened by Isla’s fever, put off by how you were spoken to, and it’s hard to get here. Let’s sort each of those.”
management.psychosocial: Saturday clinic, both children together, longer slot with a named nurse; note her concerns in the record.
sharedPlan: Isla: missed 12-month vaccines now (MMRV or MMR as she chooses), 18-month set at least 4 weeks later
Leo: pre-school booster and MMR dose 2
Fever advice and what to expect
safetyNet: If very unwell after vaccines: practice or 111
She can change her mind at any time; document decisions

pitfalls.intro: This is a communication station disguised as an immunisation quiz. Accurate facts delivered as a lecture still fail.

items.fail: Opening with risks of measles and herd immunity.
items.why: She arrived expecting judgement; a lecture confirms it.
items.fix: Ask first, then answer her specific worries.

items.fail: Not distinguishing a febrile reaction from anaphylaxis.
items.why: Only true allergy contraindicates further doses.
items.fix: Ask about swelling, breathing, rash and seizure.

items.fail: Saying the course must restart, or that MMRV is mandatory.
items.why: Both are wrong; inaccurate information erodes trust.
items.fix: Catch up without restarting; MMR available if preferred.

items.why: The access barrier is why the jabs were missed.
items.fix: Book a suitable joint appointment in the consultation.

ro.d: Follows “I’m not one of those anti-vaccine people”, “it’s complicated” and the sigh when appointment times come up.
Idea (vaccines mostly good; chickenpox better caught naturally); concern (another fever, overload, being judged, losing pay); expectation (honest answers, control, not told off).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Another frightening fever; overloading her daughter; being judged as a bad parent; losing pay — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
